rules.title: No APP privacy policy for a system that handles personal information
rules.requirement: An APP entity must have a clearly expressed and up-to-date APP privacy policy about how it manages personal information.
rules.contravention: A public-facing service collects personal information (accounts, forms, analytics, cookies) but publishes no privacy policy, or the policy does not cover the system under review (for example, a new biometric or tracking capability is not mentioned).
signals: Web or mobile front end with forms, sign-up, or analytics, and no privacy policy page, route, or link
Privacy policy exists but does not mention a capability found elsewhere in the repository (facial recognition, tracking pixels, location tracking)
exceptions: Small business operators (annual turnover of $3,000,000 or less) are generally not APP entities, unless an exception in s 6D(4) applies (for example, health service providers or businesses that trade in personal information)
rules.remediation: Publish a privacy policy that is reachable from every collection point, and update it whenever a new kind of collection is deployed.
rules.enforcement: Infringement notice or compliance notice under s 13K (up to 200 penalty units per contravention), in addition to s 13G/13H exposure.

citations.proposition: The requirement.
citations.quote: An APP entity must have a clearly expressed and up-to-date policy (the APP privacy policy) about the management of personal information by the entity.

citations.proposition: Failure to have a policy is an infringement-notice civil penalty provision.
citations.quote: Australian Privacy Principle 1.3 (requirement to have APP privacy policy);

citations.proposition: On review, the Tribunal affirmed the APP 1 contravention where the policy did not disclose the facial recognition system.
citations.quote: The Tribunal affirmed the Privacy Commissioner’s finding that Bunnings contravened Australian Privacy Principles (APP) 1 (open and transparent management of personal information) and 5 (notification of the collection of personal information) when rolling out FRT in its stores.

citations.proposition: Small business threshold (relevant to whether the APPs apply).
citations.quote: A business is a small business at a time (the test time) in a financial year (the current year) if its annual turnover for the previous financial year is $3,000,000 or less.

rules.title: APP privacy policy missing mandatory contents
rules.requirement: The policy must state the kinds of personal information collected and held, how it is collected and held, the purposes, how to seek access and correction, how to complain, whether it is likely to be disclosed overseas and, if so, the countries.
rules.contravention: A privacy policy found in the repository or deployment omits one or more of the APP 1.4 matters. The most commonly missed matter is the overseas-recipient countries when the system uses offshore hosting or SaaS.
signals: Privacy policy text lacks access/correction, complaints, or overseas-disclosure statements
Non-Australian cloud regions or offshore processors are in use but the policy names no countries
rules.remediation: Add each missing APP 1.4 matter, and list the countries of overseas recipients where it is practicable to do so.
rules.enforcement: Infringement notice or compliance notice under s 13K.

citations.proposition: The mandatory contents.
citations.quote: the APP privacy policy of the APP entity must contain the following information: (a) the kinds of personal information that the entity collects and holds; (b) how the entity collects and holds personal information; (c) the purposes for which the entity collects, holds, uses and discloses personal information;

citations.proposition: Overseas disclosure must be stated.
citations.quote: (f) whether the entity is likely to disclose personal information to overseas recipients;

citations.proposition: Infringement-notice provision.
citations.quote: Australian Privacy Principle 1.4 (contents of APP privacy policy);

rules.title: Automated decisions about individuals not disclosed in the privacy policy
rules.requirement: From 10 December 2026, if a computer program makes, or does something substantially and directly related to making, a decision that could reasonably be expected to significantly affect an individual's rights or interests using their personal information, the privacy policy must describe the kinds of personal information used and the kinds of decisions involved.
rules.contravention: The code scores, ranks, approves, refuses, prices or triages individuals (for example credit, eligibility, fraud flags, hiring, access to services), and the privacy policy does not describe automated decision-making.
signals: Model inference or rules engines whose outputs gate approvals, refusals, pricing, eligibility or account actions
Fields such as risk_score, eligibility, auto_approve or decline_reason driven by code
Privacy policy lacks any automated decision-making statement
exceptions: Applies only to decisions that could reasonably be expected to significantly affect rights or interests (APP 1.7(b)); a beneficial effect also counts (APP 1.9(c))
rules.remediation: Inventory automated decisions, then add an APP 1.8 statement covering the kinds of personal information used, the decisions made solely by programs, and the decisions substantially assisted by programs.
rules.enforcement: Infringement notice or compliance notice under s 13K once commenced. Applies to decisions made after 10 December 2026, even if the arrangement predates it (POLA Act 2024 Sch 1 item 89).

citations.proposition: The new requirement.
citations.quote: the APP privacy policy of an APP entity must contain the information covered by subclause 1.8 if: (a) the entity has arranged for a computer program to make, or do a thing that is substantially and directly related to making, a decision; and (b) the decision could reasonably be expected to significantly affect the rights or interests of an individual;

citations.proposition: Examples of decisions affecting rights or interests.
citations.quote: (ii) a decision that affects the individual’s rights under a contract, agreement or arrangement; (iii) a decision that affects the individual’s access to a significant service or support.

citations.proposition: Commencement date.
citations.quote: The day after the end of the period of 24 months beginning on the day this Act receives the Royal Assent. 10 December 2026

citations.proposition: Added to the infringement-notice list.
citations.quote: (iia) Australian Privacy Principle 1.7 (contents of APP privacy policy—automated decisions);

rules.title: Individuals forced to identify themselves where anonymity or a pseudonym would do
rules.requirement: Individuals must have the option of not identifying themselves, or of using a pseudonym, unless identification is required by law or it is impracticable to deal with them otherwise.
rules.contravention: Enquiry, feedback, survey or complaint channels make legal name, date of birth, or identity documents mandatory when the matter can be dealt with anonymously or under a pseudonym.
signals: Required full-name, DOB or ID fields on contact, feedback or survey forms
exceptions: APP 2.2: required or authorised by law or court/tribunal order, or impracticable to deal with unidentified individuals
rules.remediation: Make identity fields optional on channels that do not need them, and accept pseudonymous handles.
rules.enforcement: Infringement notice or compliance notice under s 13K.

citations.proposition: The requirement.
citations.quote: Individuals must have the option of not identifying themselves, or of using a pseudonym, when dealing with an APP entity in relation to a particular matter.

citations.proposition: Infringement-notice provision.
citations.quote: Australian Privacy Principle 2.1 (individuals may choose not to identify themselves in dealing with entities);

rules.title: Sensitive information collected with no consent mechanism
rules.requirement: Sensitive information (including health information and biometric information or templates used for automated verification or identification) may be collected only with consent and where reasonably necessary, unless an APP 3.4 exception applies.
rules.contravention: The system captures health, biometric, racial or ethnic, religious, sexual orientation, criminal record or similar data, and has no consent capture or record for that collection.
signals: Schema or form fields for health conditions, diagnoses, ethnicity, religion, sexuality or criminal history
Biometric template or face-embedding generation
No consent flag, timestamp or record linked to these fields
exceptions: APP 3.4 exceptions, including permitted general situations in s 16A (for example, suspected unlawful activity), which the ART applied in Bunnings [2026] ARTA 130
Consent may be implied, but not where the individual's intent is ambiguous
rules.remediation: Capture express, specific and current consent before collection, record it, and confirm the data is reasonably necessary. Where relying on an APP 3.4 exception, document the assessment.
rules.enforcement: Interference with privacy (s 13); determinations under s 52; civil penalty exposure under s 13G/13H for serious or repeated interferences.

citations.proposition: The requirement.
citations.quote: An APP entity must not collect sensitive information about an individual unless: (a) the individual consents to the collection of the information and:

citations.proposition: Definition includes health and biometric information.
citations.quote: (b) health information about an individual; or (c) genetic information about an individual that is not otherwise health information; or (d) biometric information that is to be used for the purpose of automated biometric verification or biometric identification;

citations.proposition: Implied consent is unavailable where intent is ambiguous.
citations.quote: Consent may not be implied if an individual’s intent is ambiguous or there is reasonable doubt about the individual’s intention.

citations.proposition: Health-website tracking pixels are a collection of sensitive information that requires consent.
citations.quote: That means website providers must obtain consent where they’re using tracking pixels to collect sensitive information, such as data on health, political opinions, race or ethnicity.

citations.proposition: Biometric templates are a distinct category of sensitive information.
citations.quote: The definition of ‘sensitive information’ extends to two particular kinds of biometric information: ‘biometric information that is to be used for the purpose of automated biometric verification or biometric identification’ and ‘biometric templates’.

rules.title: Direct marketing without a simple opt-out
rules.requirement: An organisation using personal information for direct marketing must provide a simple means for individuals to easily request not to receive direct marketing, and in some cases must draw attention to it in each communication.
rules.contravention: Marketing email, SMS or push templates and campaign code have no unsubscribe link or handling, or opt-out requests are not honoured.
signals: Templates or campaign jobs named marketing, newsletter, promo or campaign without unsubscribe/opt-out
Send paths that do not check a suppression or opt-out list
exceptions: Spam Act 2003 and Do Not Call Register Act 2006 displace APP 7 where they apply (APP 7.8)
rules.remediation: Include a functional unsubscribe in every marketing communication, and enforce a suppression list at send time.
rules.enforcement: Infringement notice or compliance notice under s 13K.

citations.proposition: Simple opt-out requirement.
citations.quote: (c) the organisation provides a simple means by which the individual may easily request not to receive direct marketing communications from the organisation;

citations.proposition: Infringement-notice provisions.
citations.quote: Australian Privacy Principle 7.2(c) or 7.3(c) (simple means for individuals to opt out of direct marketing communications);

rules.title: Government related identifier adopted as the organisation's own identifier
rules.requirement: An organisation must not adopt a government related identifier (such as a Medicare number, passport number, driver licence number, Centrelink CRN or TFN) as its own identifier of an individual unless authorised by law or regulations.
rules.contravention: A Medicare, passport, driver licence, CRN or TFN field is used as a primary key, foreign key, unique user identifier or lookup key.
signals: PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE constraints or ORM id fields on medicare_number, passport_number, licence_number, crn, tfn
Foreign keys or join keys on those fields
exceptions: APP 9.1(a): required or authorised by Australian law or court/tribunal order
APP 9.3: prescribed organisations and identifiers in regulations
rules.remediation: Generate an internal surrogate key. Store government identifiers only where needed, encrypted, and never as join keys.
rules.enforcement: Interference with privacy (s 13); s 52 determinations; s 13G/13H exposure.

citations.proposition: The prohibition.
citations.quote: An organisation must not adopt a government related identifier of an individual as its own identifier of the individual unless: (a) the adoption of the government related identifier is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order;

citations.proposition: TFNs are specifically barred from general identification use.
citations.quote: The TFN must not be used as part of a national identification system.

rules.title: Tax file numbers used, logged or retained outside authorised purposes
rules.requirement: TFN information may be used or disclosed only for purposes authorised by taxation, personal assistance or superannuation law. It must be secured, and destroyed or de-identified when no longer required.
rules.contravention: TFNs appear in logs, analytics, search indexes, test fixtures or general-purpose tables, or are kept with no destruction path.
signals: tfn / tax_file_number fields outside payroll or super modules
TFN values logged or sent to third parties
TFN-shaped values that pass the check digit, found in fixtures
exceptions: TFN recipients acting under taxation, personal assistance or superannuation law
rules.remediation: Confine TFNs to the payroll or superannuation boundary, encrypt them, exclude them from logs and analytics, and implement destruction.
rules.enforcement: Breach of a TFN rule is an interference with privacy (s 13(4)).

citations.proposition: Use and disclosure restricted.
citations.quote: TFN information must only be used or disclosed (including for matching personal information about individuals) by TFN recipients:

citations.proposition: Destruction requirement.
citations.quote: A TFN recipient must take reasonable steps to securely destroy or permanently de-identify TFN information where it is no longer:

rules.title: Personal information in publicly accessible storage
rules.requirement: Reasonable steps, including technical and organisational measures, must be taken to protect personal information from unauthorised access or disclosure.
rules.contravention: Infrastructure-as-code makes storage that holds or may hold personal information world-readable: public buckets or containers, public ACLs, disabled public-access blocks, or publicly accessible databases.
signals: S3 acl = public-read or public-read-write; block_public_acls = false
GCS allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers bindings
Azure container public access
publicly_accessible = true on RDS
exceptions: Genuinely public, non-personal assets (marketing images, static site bundles). Confirm the bucket cannot receive personal information.
rules.remediation: Block public access at account and bucket level, serve public assets through a CDN origin identity, and restrict database ingress to private networks.
rules.enforcement: Interference with privacy; APP 11.1 failures supported the first civil penalties ($4.2m of $5.8m in ACL [2025] FCA 1224).

citations.proposition: The security obligation.
citations.quote: If an APP entity holds personal information, the entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to protect the information: (a) from misuse, interference and loss; and (b) from unauthorised access, modification or disclosure.

citations.proposition: Reasonable steps include technical measures (inserted by POLA Act 2024).
citations.quote: For the purposes of subclauses 11.1 and 11.2, without limiting those subclauses or any other provision of this Act, such steps include technical and organisational measures.

citations.proposition: APP 11.1 can be contravened without proof that an unauthorised disclosure actually occurred.
citations.quote: it not necessary for me to first be satisfied that unauthorised disclosure has in fact occurred to make a finding that the respondent has contravened APP 11.1.

citations.proposition: APP 11.1 failures attracted civil penalties, counted per individual.
citations.quote: a penalty of $4.2 million for ACL's failure to take reasonable steps to protect the personal information held by ACL on Medlab Pathology’s IT systems under Australian Privacy Principle 11.1, which amounted to more than to 223,000 contraventions of s 13G(a) of the Privacy Act;

rules.title: Credentials stored or handled in a way that defeats access control
rules.requirement: As for APP 11.1: technical measures appropriate to the risk.
rules.contravention: Passwords are stored in plaintext or with fast unsalted hashes (MD5, SHA-1, unsalted SHA-256), or live secrets granting access to personal information stores are committed to the repository.
signals: md5(password) / sha1(password) / hashlib.sha256(password)
AWS access keys, private keys, database URLs with passwords committed
Password columns without a hashing library
exceptions: Test-only dummy credentials that cannot access real systems (confirm, then move to a secret store anyway)
rules.remediation: Use a memory-hard password hash (argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt), rotate any committed secret immediately, and move secrets to a managed secret store.
rules.enforcement: Interference with privacy; s 13G/13H exposure where a breach follows.

citations.proposition: The security obligation.
citations.quote: If an APP entity holds personal information, the entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to protect the information: (a) from misuse, interference and loss; and (b) from unauthorised access, modification or disclosure.

citations.proposition: Sophisticated entities are expected to address known and persistent security risks.
citations.quote: this determination provides further guidance on the application of APP 11.1 to the conduct of highly sophisticated regulated entities, and in particular with respect to expectations as to steps required to be taken to address and mitigate known and persistent security risks.

citations.proposition: ALLEGED ONLY: stolen credentials alone sufficed to reach the corporate network.
citations.quote: The threat actor was able to authenticate and log onto Medibank’s Global Protect VPN using only the Medibank Credentials because, during the Relevant Period, access to Medibank’s Global Protect VPN did not require two or more proofs of identity or multi-factor authentication (MFA).

rules.title: Personal information sent without transport security
rules.requirement: As for APP 11.1: technical measures appropriate to the risk.
rules.contravention: TLS certificate verification is disabled in production code, or personal information is sent to non-local http:// endpoints, or forms post over plain HTTP.
signals: verify=False, rejectUnauthorized: false, InsecureSkipVerify: true, NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0
http:// API base URLs that are not localhost
<form action="http://...">
exceptions: Local development or test endpoints (localhost, 127.0.0.1, *.local, *.test)
rules.remediation: Enforce TLS with verification, set HSTS, and fail closed.
rules.enforcement: Interference with privacy; s 13G/13H exposure where a breach follows.

citations.proposition: Technical measures are part of reasonable steps.
citations.quote: For the purposes of subclauses 11.1 and 11.2, without limiting those subclauses or any other provision of this Act, such steps include technical and organisational measures.

citations.proposition: No need to prove that interception occurred.
citations.quote: it not necessary for me to first be satisfied that unauthorised disclosure has in fact occurred to make a finding that the respondent has contravened APP 11.1.

rules.title: Collection with no notice at or before the point of collection
rules.requirement: At or before collection (or as soon as practicable after), reasonable steps must be taken to notify the individual of the APP 5.2 matters, including the entity's identity, the purposes, the consequences of not providing the information, and overseas disclosure.
rules.contravention: Forms, sensors, cameras or SDKs collect personal information with no collection notice in the flow. Signage or text that says collection 'may' occur is not adequate notice of actual biometric collection.
signals: Forms collecting personal information with no adjacent notice or privacy link
Camera, biometric or tracking features with no in-flow notice
Notice copy using hedged language such as 'may include facial recognition'
exceptions: Where no steps are reasonable in the circumstances (APP 5.1 'if any')
rules.remediation: Put a layered collection notice at the point of collection that states plainly what is collected, why, by whom, and where it goes.
rules.enforcement: Interference with privacy; s 52 determinations.

citations.proposition: The requirement.

Exports of login or verification history to marketing or data warehouses

Compliance with the Digital ID Act, or use required or authorised by law (s 53(3)(b), (c))

heuristics.title: Facial recognition or biometric matching of the general public
heuristics.concern: Matching faces (or other biometrics) of everyone in a space, to find a few people of interest, has repeatedly been found to collect sensitive information without consent. Exceptions survive only where a documented assessment shows suitability, effectiveness, no less intrusive alternative, and proportionality.
heuristics.reasoning: 7-Eleven, Clearview, Kmart and Bunnings all turned on indiscriminate biometric collection. On review in Bunnings, the ART accepted that a permitted general situation could apply, but it kept the OAIC's test (suitability, alternatives, proportionality), held that momentary collection is still collection, and affirmed the notice and governance failures. The safe inference is that facial recognition on the public is presumptively unlawful unless the deployer can evidence a structured, documented proportionality assessment, gives specific notice, and limits the system's scope and retention.
signals: face_recognition, dlib, insightface, deepface, OpenCV face detectors feeding a matcher
AWS Rekognition IndexFaces / SearchFacesByImage, Azure Face identify, Google Vision face matching
Watchlists, enrolment galleries, or embeddings stored for faces
questions_for_agent: Is matching one-to-many (identification) or one-to-one with an enrolled, consenting user (verification)?
Is there a documented assessment of suitability, alternatives and proportionality?
Are non-matched templates discarded immediately, and is that verified?
Does the notice say plainly that facial recognition is in use?
heuristics.remediation: Prefer one-to-one verification with express consent. If identification is unavoidable, document the s 16A assessment, give specific notice, discard non-matches immediately, and audit vendor defaults.

heuristics.title: Third-party tracking pixels on health or other sensitive-context pages
heuristics.concern: Advertising and analytics pixels on pages that reveal health, sexuality, religion, ethnicity or similar context collect and disclose sensitive information to the platform. That requires consent, and in practice the disclosure is to an overseas recipient.
heuristics.reasoning: In the 2026 Monash IVF and Medmate determinations, the OAIC held that tracking health-site visitors for targeted advertising is a collection of sensitive information requiring consent. Combined with Telstra (information can be 'about' a person in combination) and Facebook (setting cookies on Australian devices is conduct in Australia), the inference is that page URLs, events and hashed identifiers sent to ad platforms are personal and, in sensitive contexts, sensitive information.
signals: Meta Pixel (fbq, connect.facebook.net/*/fbevents.js)
TikTok, LinkedIn Insight, Snap, Pinterest, Reddit, X (Twitter) pixels
Google Ads conversion / gtag with ads identifiers; Floodlight
Advanced matching that sends hashed emails or phone numbers
Repository context suggesting health, fertility, mental health, sexual health, pharmacy, disability, religion or similar

Is consent obtained before the pixel fires (not just a banner)?
Are hashed identifiers sent (advanced matching, CAPI)?
heuristics.remediation: Remove ad pixels from sensitive-context pages, or gate them behind prior opt-in consent. Disable advanced matching, strip URLs and query strings, and record the countries of ad-platform recipients in the privacy policy.

heuristics.title: Scraping personal information because it is publicly available
heuristics.concern: Publicly accessible does not mean free to collect. Bulk scraping of profiles, images or contact details is usually covert, so it fails the fair-means test, and images used for matching are sensitive.
heuristics.reasoning: Clearview was found to have collected by unfair means and without consent, despite its argument that the sources were public and that it respected robots.txt. The determination stands after the AAT review. Regulators' joint statement treats mass scraping as a privacy issue for both scrapers and the sites scraped.

Storage of scraped names, images, emails or phone numbers
Face embeddings built from scraped images
questions_for_agent: What personal information is extracted and stored?
Would individuals expect the collection, and are they notified?
heuristics.remediation: Do not collect personal information by scraping unless there is a lawful, fair basis and notice. Minimise fields, and do not build biometric templates from scraped images.

citations.proposition: The fair-means test.

heuristics.title: Form or schema collects more than the function needs
heuristics.concern: Fields such as gender, date of birth, dependants, citizenship or visa status, prior addresses, marital status or employment history, collected by default or as required fields, may not be reasonably necessary, especially where the individual is in a weaker bargaining position.
heuristics.reasoning: In IRE (2Apply) the Commissioner ordered a rental application platform to stop collecting a list of fields that were not reasonably necessary, and treated the market's power imbalance as relevant to fairness. The determination is under ART review, so treat it as a strong indicator, not settled law.
signals: Required fields: gender, dob, dependants, citizenship, visa_status/visa_expiry, marital_status, previous_addresses, bankruptcy, student_status
Collection at the first step of a multi-stage process when the data is needed only later
questions_for_agent: For each field, which function needs it, and at which stage?
Is the user in a position to refuse (rental, employment, essential services)?
heuristics.remediation: Justify each field against a function. Make fields optional or defer them to the stage that needs them, and delete what is not used.

citations.quote: collecting personal information that is not reasonably necessary for its functions or activities, in breach of Australian Privacy Principle (APP) 3.2; and b. collecting personal information by unfair means, in breach of APP 3.5.

heuristics.title: Consent obtained through bundling, pre-ticked boxes, or pressure design
heuristics.concern: Consent that is bundled into terms or a privacy policy, pre-selected, or extracted through manipulative interface design (confirmshaming, forced continuity, asymmetric buttons) may not be valid. The design itself can make collection unfair.
heuristics.reasoning: Flight Centre: general privacy policy statements, bundled with other purposes, were not consent. 7-Eleven: implied consent fails where intent is ambiguous. IRE: online choice architecture that pressures individuals bore on whether collection was fair (under review).

Single checkbox agreeing to terms + privacy + marketing
Decline copy such as 'No thanks, I don't care about'
questions_for_agent: Is each purpose consented to separately?
Is declining as easy as accepting?
heuristics.remediation: Use unbundled, unticked, purpose-specific consent with an equally prominent decline option, and record what was agreed and when.

heuristics.title: Real personal information in test, demo, training, fixture or shared datasets
heuristics.concern: Copies of production data in fixtures, seeds, notebooks, demo or training databases, or files shared with vendors and hackathons carry production's privacy risk, often without production's controls. Synthetic data removes the risk; a production copy needs production-grade safeguards.
heuristics.reasoning: Flight Centre gave hackathon teams a dataset that still contained credit card and passport details despite de-identification checks; the Commissioner found unauthorised disclosure and inadequate security and governance. DMP (NSW tribunal, HPP 5) limits the point: a snapshot of a hospital's medical-record system used for training and testing was not a breach, because the safeguards taken as a whole (restricted access, continuous access auditing, signed declarations, two-factor remote access) were reasonable. The tribunal doubted shared generic logins and observed that mock records would have avoided any breach. The question is therefore whether the copy is synthetic or masked, and if not, whether it is controlled like production.
signals: Fixtures or seeds with realistic names, real-looking emails (non-example domains), AU mobiles, valid-checksum card numbers, TFNs or Medicare numbers
Database dumps (*.sql, *.csv, *.parquet) in the repository
Notebooks with output cells showing personal data
questions_for_agent: Was the data synthesised, masked, or copied from production?
Who else received the dataset?
Is access to the non-production copy restricted, attributed to individual users, and audited?
Is MFA enforced on remote access to it, and how long is each copy retained?
heuristics.remediation: Use synthetic or masked data by default. Where a production copy is unavoidable, apply production access controls, per-user credentials, access auditing and MFA, and retire copies on a schedule. Block dumps with pre-commit hooks and treat any de-identification as needing independent verification.

citations.proposition: Facts.
citations.quote: Participants were given access to a dataset which included customers’ personal information, despite preliminary checks to de-identify or remove personal information.

citations.proposition: Plan for human error.
citations.quote: Organisations should assume that human errors – such as the inadvertent disclosure of personal information to suppliers – could occur and take steps to prevent them.

heuristics.title: Personal information retained with no destruction or de-identification path
heuristics.concern: Systems that keep personal information indefinitely, with no TTL, lifecycle rule, purge job or retention policy, enlarge breach impact and fail APP 11.2 once the data is no longer needed.
heuristics.reasoning: Uber was found to have failed to destroy or de-identify data as required, and was ordered to adopt a retention and destruction policy. IRE's investigation scope included retention. Breach penalties count each affected individual (ACL), so retained data directly scales exposure.
signals: Personal-information tables and buckets without TTL, expiry, lifecycle or purge logic
No retention policy document
questions_for_agent: What is the retention period for each data class, and what enforces it?

heuristics.concern: Suppressed security findings, 'TODO: fix auth' comments, disabled checks and long-lived exceptions are evidence that risks were known. Decisions now treat knowledge of a persistent risk as aggravating.
heuristics.reasoning: Optus (White Pages): APP 11.1 expectations focus on known and persistent risks. Vinomofo: the entity was aware of its security deficiencies years before the incident. ACL: senior management involvement in the decisions was noted in the first civil penalty case.

TODO/FIXME/HACK comments mentioning auth, encryption, PII, security or MFA
Security scanners disabled in CI

citations.proposition: Known and persistent risks.

heuristics.title: Remote or administrative access to personal information without MFA or least privilege
heuristics.concern: Single-factor access to VPNs, admin consoles, identity providers or databases holding personal information, and broad standing privileges, are the access paths behind the largest Australian breaches.
heuristics.reasoning: The Commissioner's pleaded case against Medibank alleges that a VPN without MFA, and weak privileged-access controls, were failures to take reasonable steps. These are ALLEGATIONS, not findings, but they show what the regulator will argue are reasonable steps. One decided state authority points the same way: in DMP (NSW tribunal, HPP 5) two-factor authentication on remote access was described as a standard security tool within a reasonable suite of safeguards, and shared generic logins without per-user attribution were said to be insufficient on their own. EQH treated need-to-know access as part of a reasonable safeguard set.
signals: Cognito mfa_configuration = OFF; Auth0/Okta/Keycloak policies without MFA for admins
Admin routes protected only by password
IAM policies with Action '*' on data stores
questions_for_agent: Is MFA enforced for every remote and privileged path to personal information?
heuristics.remediation: Enforce phishing-resistant MFA on remote and privileged access, apply least privilege, review privileged accounts regularly, and monitor them.

citations.proposition: ALLEGED: VPN access without MFA.
citations.quote: access to Medibank’s Global Protect VPN did not require two or more proofs of identity or multi-factor authentication (MFA).

heuristics.title: No capability to assess and notify an eligible data breach on time
heuristics.concern: Without logging, a runbook, and named owners, an entity cannot complete a reasonable and expeditious assessment within 30 days or notify as soon as practicable. Both failures now attract separate penalties.
heuristics.reasoning: ACL was penalised separately for the assessment (s 26WH(2)) and notification (s 26WK(2)) failures, as well as for APP 11.1. Uber took almost a year to assess. Optus v Robertson shows that forensic reports commissioned for several purposes may not be privileged, which affects how incident documentation should be planned.

No audit logging on data-access paths
No mention of the 30-day assessment window or OAIC notification

heuristics.remediation: Maintain an NDB runbook (assess within 30 days; notify as soon as practicable; s 26WK(3) statement contents), keep access logs that can scope exfiltration, and rehearse the process.

heuristics.title: Personal information hosted or processed offshore (cloud regions, SaaS, AI APIs)
heuristics.concern: Using non-Australian regions or overseas processors (analytics, error tracking, CRM, LLM APIs) usually discloses personal information to overseas recipients. The entity remains accountable for their conduct (s 16C), and must name the countries in its policy and notices.
heuristics.reasoning: Uber: transfer of Australians' data to US servers within the corporate group, and the Act applied to the overseas companies. Facebook: the Act can reach foreign entities through an Australian link, including cookie operations. Clearview: business integral to the service was carried on in Australia. The inference runs both ways: offshore processing does not avoid the Act, and Australian entities carry their recipients' risk.

SDKs for Sentry, Datadog, Segment, Mixpanel, Amplitude, Intercom, HubSpot, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini and similar receiving user data

Are there contractual APP-equivalent protections (APP 8.1 reasonable steps)?
heuristics.remediation: Prefer AU regions for personal-information stores. Where offshore processing is needed, put APP-equivalent contract terms in place, minimise or redact data before sending, and list the countries in the privacy policy and collection notices.

heuristics.title: Device IDs, IP addresses, hashed emails and event streams treated as non-personal
heuristics.concern: Systems often assume that hashed emails, advertising IDs, IP addresses or session streams are anonymous. Whether information is about a reasonably identifiable individual is an evaluative, contextual question, and combination can make it personal.
heuristics.reasoning: Telstra (Full Court): 'about an individual' is evaluative and can be met in combination. The pixel determinations applied this to online identifiers used to target individuals. Hashing for matching is pseudonymisation, not de-identification. NSW tribunals apply Telstra to the NSW definition and accept that identity can be ascertained by combining the information with other information, including information the organisation itself publishes (Stalvies, summarising APV & APW).
signals: sha256(email) or md5(email) sent to third parties
IP, device or ad IDs logged with user events
'anonymous' or 'anonymised' labels on datasets that contain stable IDs
questions_for_agent: Could the recipient link the identifier to a person, alone or with other data it holds?
heuristics.remediation: Treat stable identifiers as personal information, apply APP 6 and APP 11 to them, and use real aggregation or noise if de-identification is claimed.

heuristics.title: Location collection that does not match what settings and notices suggest
heuristics.concern: Precise or background location collected through paths other than the obvious location setting misleads users. That has been found to contravene the Australian Consumer Law, and it bears on fairness and notice under the APPs.
heuristics.reasoning: ACCC v Google: users who turned 'Location History' off were misled while 'Web & App Activity' kept collecting location. The penalty followed in 2022. This is a consumer-law case, applied here by analogy to APP 3.5 and APP 5. No privacy decision on location tracking stands in this knowledge base: the NSW tribunal's Opal-card travel-history finding (Waters v Transport for NSW [2018] NSWCATAD 40) was set aside on appeal (Transport for NSW v Waters [2018] NSWCATAP 200).

Location captured in analytics events or with other toggles

heuristics.remediation: Have one authoritative location control that governs every collection path, use coarse location by default, and describe it plainly in the notice.

heuristics.title: Session recording, keystroke capture, covert recording or exposure of private information (statutory tort)
heuristics.concern: Features that record users' screens or keystrokes, covertly capture audio or video, or expose private information can amount to intrusion upon seclusion or misuse of information under the statutory tort. The tort is actionable without proof of damage and is not limited to APP entities, so small businesses are included.
heuristics.reasoning: Schedule 2 created a cause of action that the High Court in Lenah Game Meats declined to recognise at common law. There is little tort case law so far, so this is an exposure flag, not a predicted outcome.

Employee monitoring agents

heuristics.title: Staff access to personal records without need-to-know limits, per-user attribution or audit
heuristics.concern: Staff browsing records they have no work reason to see is a recurring source of privacy complaints. Systems that give every staff user access to every record, use shared logins, or cannot show who looked at what leave the organisation unable to prevent, detect or answer for it.
heuristics.reasoning: NSW tribunals have accepted as reasonable safeguards against staff intrusion: making staff aware of their obligations, limiting access to those who need it for their duties, telling staff their access is monitored, audit trails that identify the individual user, and acting on misuse (EQH, FQW). Shared generic logins that cannot attribute access are insufficient on their own (DMP). The NSW cases also held the agency not responsible for an employee's browsing outside her duties. That outcome does not transfer: under the Privacy Act, acts of employees in the performance of their duties are treated as the entity's own (s 8(1)(a)), so the safeguard set is the transferable lesson, not the defence.
signals: Staff or admin consoles over personal-information tables with no role or relationship checks on record access
Shared, generic, training or demo accounts with access to real records
No read-access audit (no access-log middleware, database audit extension, or object-level data events on stores holding personal information)
questions_for_agent: Can staff open any record, or only records they need for their role?
Is every read of personal information attributable to an individual user and retained in an audit log?
Are staff told access is monitored, and is the log ever reviewed?
heuristics.remediation: Enforce need-to-know (role- and relationship-based) access, give every person their own credentials, log reads of personal information with the user's identity, tell staff access is monitored, review logs proactively for high-risk records, and act on misuse.

heuristics.title: Automated bulk sending of personal reports or attachments without recipient verification
heuristics.concern: Pipelines that generate per-person reports and email them to a mapped list of recipients can send thousands of records to the wrong people in one run. Unencrypted attachments, sample-based checks and reliance on recipients to behave well do not prevent it.
heuristics.reasoning: In FMM a misalignment sent 191,870 claims reports to the wrong employers. The tribunal held that the scale called for stringent safeguards; that sampling checks, annual training, cover-page disclaimers and recipients' own obligations were weak; that the agency's responsibility could not be delegated to recipients; and that an authenticated portal would eliminate misdirection. On appeal the security contravention was confirmed (s 12(c) PPIP Act, HPP 5) but the disclosure findings were set aside: in NSW, information is disclosed only if it is made known, and the attachment was deleted unread. Under the Privacy Act the robust basis for a misdirection finding is therefore APP 11.1; whether APP 6 is also engaged depends on the facts.
signals: Loops that attach generated files per recipient (SES SendRawEmail, nodemailer attachments, smtplib with MIMEApplication) built from database rows
Recipient-to-report mapping tables maintained by hand or joined on mutable keys
Attachments not encrypted or password protected; no authenticated download alternative
questions_for_agent: How is the recipient for each report determined, and is the mapping independently verified before sending?
Could recipients instead authenticate to a portal to retrieve their reports?
Are attachments encrypted, and is there a hold-and-check step before a bulk run is released?
heuristics.remediation: Replace bulk attachments with authenticated retrieval. Until then, verify every recipient mapping before release (not by sampling), encrypt attachments, stage bulk runs behind a two-person release check, and monitor for stale addresses.

1.title: open and transparent management of personal information
1.text:
1  Australian Privacy Principle 1—open and transparent management of personal information
 1.1 The object of this principle is to ensure that APP entities manage personal information in an open and transparent way.
Compliance with the Australian Privacy Principles etc.
 1.2 An APP entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to implement practices, procedures and systems relating to the entity’s functions or activities that:
 (a) will ensure that the entity complies with the Australian Privacy Principles and a registered APP code (if any) that binds the entity; and
 (b) will enable the entity to deal with inquiries or complaints from individuals about the entity’s compliance with the Australian Privacy Principles or such a code.
APP Privacy policy
 1.3 An APP entity must have a clearly expressed and up‑to‑date policy (the APP privacy policy) about the management of personal information by the entity.
 1.4 Without limiting subclause 1.3, the APP privacy policy of the APP entity must contain the following information:
 (a) the kinds of personal information that the entity collects and holds;
 (b) how the entity collects and holds personal information;
 (c) the purposes for which the entity collects, holds, uses and discloses personal information;
 (d) how an individual may access personal information about the individual that is held by the entity and seek the correction of such information;
 (e) how an individual may complain about a breach of the Australian Privacy Principles, or a registered APP code (if any) that binds the entity, and how the entity will deal with such a complaint;
 (f) whether the entity is likely to disclose personal information to overseas recipients;
 (g) if the entity is likely to disclose personal information to overseas recipients—the countries in which such recipients are likely to be located if it is practicable to specify those countries in the policy.
Availability of APP privacy policy etc.
 1.5 An APP entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to make its APP privacy policy available:
 (a) free of charge; and
 (b) in such form as is appropriate.
Note: An APP entity will usually make its APP privacy policy available on the entity’s website.
 1.6 If a person or body requests a copy of the APP privacy policy of an APP entity in a particular form, the entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to give the person or body a copy in that form.

future.text:
Automated decisions
 1.7 Without limiting subclause 1.3, the APP privacy policy of an APP entity must contain the information covered by subclause 1.8 if:
 (a) the entity has arranged for a computer program to make, or do a thing that is substantially and directly related to making, a decision; and
 (b) the decision could reasonably be expected to significantly affect the rights or interests of an individual; and
 (c) personal information about the individual is used in the operation of the computer program to make the decision or do the thing that is substantially and directly related to making the decision.
 1.8 The information covered by this subclause is:
 (a) the kinds of personal information used in the operation of such computer programs; and
 (b) the kinds of such decisions made solely by the operation of such computer programs; and
 (c) the kinds of such decisions for which a thing, that is substantially and directly related to making the decision, is done by the operation of such computer programs.
 1.9 For the purposes of subclauses 1.7 and 1.8:
 (a) making a decision includes refusing or failing to make a decision; and
 (b) doing a thing includes refusing or failing to do a thing; and
 (c) a decision may affect the rights or interests of an individual, whether the rights or interests of the individual are adversely or beneficially affected; and
 (d) the following are examples of the kinds of decisions that may affect the rights or interests of an individual:
 (i) a decision made under a provision of an Act or a legislative instrument to grant, or to refuse to grant, a benefit to the individual;
 (ii) a decision that affects the individual’s rights under a contract, agreement or arrangement;
 (iii) a decision that affects the individual’s access to a significant service or support.

2.title: anonymity and pseudonymity
2.text:
2  Australian Privacy Principle 2—anonymity and pseudonymity
 2.1 Individuals must have the option of not identifying themselves, or of using a pseudonym, when dealing with an APP entity in relation to a particular matter.
 2.2 Subclause 2.1 does not apply if, in relation to that matter:
 (a) the APP entity is required or authorised by or under an Australian law, or a court/tribunal order, to deal with individuals who have identified themselves; or
 (b) it is impracticable for the APP entity to deal with individuals who have not identified themselves or who have used a pseudonym.
Part 2—Collection of personal information

3.title: collection of solicited personal information
3.text:
3  Australian Privacy Principle 3—collection of solicited personal information
Personal information other than sensitive information
 3.1 If an APP entity is an agency, the entity must not collect personal information (other than sensitive information) unless the information is reasonably necessary for, or directly related to, one or more of the entity’s functions or activities.
 3.2 If an APP entity is an organisation, the entity must not collect personal information (other than sensitive information) unless the information is reasonably necessary for one or more of the entity’s functions or activities.
Sensitive information
 3.3 An APP entity must not collect sensitive information about an individual unless:
 (a) the individual consents to the collection of the information and:
 (i) if the entity is an agency—the information is reasonably necessary for, or directly related to, one or more of the entity’s functions or activities; or
 (ii) if the entity is an organisation—the information is reasonably necessary for one or more of the entity’s functions or activities; or
 (b) subclause 3.4 applies in relation to the information.
 3.4 This subclause applies in relation to sensitive information about an individual if:
 (a) the collection of the information is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order; or
 (b) a permitted general situation exists in relation to the collection of the information by the APP entity; or
 (c) the APP entity is an organisation and a permitted health situation exists in relation to the collection of the information by the entity; or
 (d) the APP entity is an enforcement body and the entity reasonably believes that:
 (i) if the entity is the Immigration Department—the collection of the information is reasonably necessary for, or directly related to, one or more enforcement related activities conducted by, or on behalf of, the entity; or
 (ii) otherwise—the collection of the information is reasonably necessary for, or directly related to, one or more of the entity’s functions or activities; or
 (e) the APP entity is a non‑profit organisation and both of the following apply:
 (i) the information relates to the activities of the organisation;
 (ii) the information relates solely to the members of the organisation, or to individuals who have regular contact with the organisation in connection with its activities.
Note: For permitted general situation, see section 16A. For permitted health situation, see section 16B.
Means of collection
 3.5 An APP entity must collect personal information only by lawful and fair means.
 3.6 An APP entity must collect personal information about an individual only from the individual unless:
 (a) if the entity is an agency:
 (i) the individual consents to the collection of the information from someone other than the individual; or
 (ii) the entity is required or authorised by or under an Australian law, or a court/tribunal order, to collect the information from someone other than the individual; or
 (b) it is unreasonable or impracticable to do so.
Solicited personal information
 3.7 This principle applies to the collection of personal information that is solicited by an APP entity.

4.title: dealing with unsolicited personal information
4.text:
4  Australian Privacy Principle 4—dealing with unsolicited personal information
 4.1 If:
 (a) an APP entity receives personal information; and
 (b) the entity did not solicit the information;
the entity must, within a reasonable period after receiving the information, determine whether or not the entity could have collected the information under Australian Privacy Principle 3 if the entity had solicited the information.
 4.2 The APP entity may use or disclose the personal information for the purposes of making the determination under subclause 4.1.
 4.3 If:
 (a) the APP entity determines that the entity could not have collected the personal information; and
 (b) the information is not contained in a Commonwealth record;
the entity must, as soon as practicable but only if it is lawful and reasonable to do so, destroy the information or ensure that the information is de‑identified.
 4.4 If subclause 4.3 does not apply in relation to the personal information, Australian Privacy Principles 5 to 13 apply in relation to the information as if the entity had collected the information under Australian Privacy Principle 3.

5.title: notification of the collection of personal information

6.title: use or disclosure of personal information
6.text:
6  Australian Privacy Principle 6—use or disclosure of personal information
Use or disclosure
 6.1 If an APP entity holds personal information about an individual that was collected for a particular purpose (the primary purpose), the entity must not use or disclose the information for another purpose (the secondary purpose) unless:
 (a) the individual has consented to the use or disclosure of the information; or
 (b) subclause 6.2 or 6.3 applies in relation to the use or disclosure of the information.
Note: Australian Privacy Principle 8 sets out requirements for the disclosure of personal information to a person who is not in Australia or an external Territory.
 6.2 This subclause applies in relation to the use or disclosure of personal information about an individual if:
 (a) the individual would reasonably expect the APP entity to use or disclose the information for the secondary purpose and the secondary purpose is:
 (i) if the information is sensitive information—directly related to the primary purpose; or
 (ii) if the information is not sensitive information—related to the primary purpose; or
 (b) the use or disclosure of the information is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order; or
 (c) a permitted general situation exists in relation to the use or disclosure of the information by the APP entity; or
 (d) the APP entity is an organisation and a permitted health situation exists in relation to the use or disclosure of the information by the entity; or
 (e) the APP entity reasonably believes that the use or disclosure of the information is reasonably necessary for one or more enforcement related activities conducted by, or on behalf of, an enforcement body.
Note: For permitted general situation, see section 16A. For permitted health situation, see section 16B.
 6.3 This subclause applies in relation to the disclosure of personal information about an individual by an APP entity that is an agency if:
 (a) the agency is not an enforcement body; and
 (b) the information is biometric information or biometric templates; and
 (c) the recipient of the information is an enforcement body; and
 (d) the disclosure is conducted in accordance with the guidelines made by the Commissioner for the purposes of this paragraph.
 6.4 If:
 (a) the APP entity is an organisation; and
 (b) subsection 16B(2) applied in relation to the collection of the personal information by the entity;
the entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure that the information is de‑identified before the entity discloses it in accordance with subclause 6.1 or 6.2.
Written note of use or disclosure
 6.5 If an APP entity uses or discloses personal information in accordance with paragraph 6.2(e), the entity must make a written note of the use or disclosure.
Related bodies corporate
 6.6 If:
 (a) an APP entity is a body corporate; and
 (b) the entity collects personal information from a related body corporate;
this principle applies as if the entity’s primary purpose for the collection of the information were the primary purpose for which the related body corporate collected the information.
Exceptions
 6.7 This principle does not apply to the use or disclosure by an organisation of:
 (a) personal information for the purpose of direct marketing; or
 (b) government related identifiers.

7.title: direct marketing
7.text:
7  Australian Privacy Principle 7—direct marketing
Direct marketing
 7.1 If an organisation holds personal information about an individual, the organisation must not use or disclose the information for the purpose of direct marketing.
Note: An act or practice of an agency may be treated as an act or practice of an organisation, see section 7A.
Exceptions—personal information other than sensitive information
 7.2 Despite subclause 7.1, an organisation may use or disclose personal information (other than sensitive information) about an individual for the purpose of direct marketing if:
 (a) the organisation collected the information from the individual; and
 (b) the individual would reasonably expect the organisation to use or disclose the information for that purpose; and
 (c) the organisation provides a simple means by which the individual may easily request not to receive direct marketing communications from the organisation; and
 (d) the individual has not made such a request to the organisation.
 7.3 Despite subclause 7.1, an organisation may use or disclose personal information (other than sensitive information) about an individual for the purpose of direct marketing if:
 (a) the organisation collected the information from:
 (i) the individual and the individual would not reasonably expect the organisation to use or disclose the information for that purpose; or
 (ii) someone other than the individual; and
 (b) either:
 (i) the individual has consented to the use or disclosure of the information for that purpose; or
 (ii) it is impracticable to obtain that consent; and
 (c) the organisation provides a simple means by which the individual may easily request not to receive direct marketing communications from the organisation; and
 (d) in each direct marketing communication with the individual:
 (i) the organisation includes a prominent statement that the individual may make such a request; or
 (ii) the organisation otherwise draws the individual’s attention to the fact that the individual may make such a request; and
 (e) the individual has not made such a request to the organisation.
Exception—sensitive information
 7.4 Despite subclause 7.1, an organisation may use or disclose sensitive information about an individual for the purpose of direct marketing if the individual has consented to the use or disclosure of the information for that purpose.
Exception—contracted service providers
 7.5 Despite subclause 7.1, an organisation may use or disclose personal information for the purpose of direct marketing if:
 (a) the organisation is a contracted service provider for a Commonwealth contract; and
 (b) the organisation collected the information for the purpose of meeting (directly or indirectly) an obligation under the contract; and
 (c) the use or disclosure is necessary to meet (directly or indirectly) such an obligation.
Individual may request not to receive direct marketing communications etc.
 7.6 If an organisation (the first organisation) uses or discloses personal information about an individual:
 (a) for the purpose of direct marketing by the first organisation; or
 (b) for the purpose of facilitating direct marketing by other organisations;
the individual may:
 (c) if paragraph (a) applies—request not to receive direct marketing communications from the first organisation; and
 (d) if paragraph (b) applies—request the organisation not to use or disclose the information for the purpose referred to in that paragraph; and
 (e) request the first organisation to provide its source of the information.
 7.7 If an individual makes a request under subclause 7.6, the first organisation must not charge the individual for the making of, or to give effect to, the request and:
 (a) if the request is of a kind referred to in paragraph 7.6(c) or (d)—the first organisation must give effect to the request within a reasonable period after the request is made; and
 (b) if the request is of a kind referred to in paragraph 7.6(e)—the organisation must, within a reasonable period after the request is made, notify the individual of its source unless it is impracticable or unreasonable to do so.
Interaction with other legislation
 7.8 This principle does not apply to the extent that any of the following apply:
 (aa) Division 5 of Part 7B of the Interactive Gambling Act 2001;
 (a) the Do Not Call Register Act 2006;
 (b) the Spam Act 2003;
 (c) any other Act of the Commonwealth, or a law in force in an external Territory, prescribed by the regulations.

8.title: cross‑border disclosure of personal information
8.text:
8  Australian Privacy Principle 8—cross‑border disclosure of personal information
 8.1 Before an APP entity discloses personal information about an individual to a person (the overseas recipient):
 (a) who is not in Australia or an external Territory; and
 (b) who is not the entity or the individual;
the entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure that the overseas recipient does not breach the Australian Privacy Principles (other than Australian Privacy Principle 1) in relation to the information.
Note: In certain circumstances, an act done, or a practice engaged in, by the overseas recipient is taken, under section 16C, to have been done, or engaged in, by the APP entity and to be a breach of the Australian Privacy Principles.
 8.2 Subclause 8.1 does not apply to the disclosure of personal information about an individual by an APP entity to the overseas recipient if:
 (a) the entity reasonably believes that:
 (i) the recipient of the information is subject to a law, or binding scheme, that has the effect of protecting the information in a way that, overall, is at least substantially similar to the way in which the Australian Privacy Principles protect the information; and
 (ii) there are mechanisms that the individual can access to take action to enforce that protection of the law or binding scheme; or
 (aa) subclause 8.3 applies in relation to the disclosure of the information; or
 (b) both of the following apply:
 (i) the entity expressly informs the individual that if he or she consents to the disclosure of the information, subclause 8.1 will not apply to the disclosure;
 (ii) after being so informed, the individual consents to the disclosure; or
 (c) the disclosure of the information is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order; or
 (d) a permitted general situation (other than the situation referred to in item 4 or 5 of the table in subsection 16A(1)) exists in relation to the disclosure of the information by the APP entity; or
 (e) the entity is an agency and the disclosure of the information is required or authorised by or under an international agreement relating to information sharing to which Australia is a party; or
 (f) the entity is an agency and both of the following apply:
 (i) the entity reasonably believes that the disclosure of the information is reasonably necessary for one or more enforcement related activities conducted by, or on behalf of, an enforcement body;
 (ii) the recipient is a body that performs functions, or exercises powers, that are similar to those performed or exercised by an enforcement body.
Note: For permitted general situation, see section 16A.
 8.3 This subclause applies in relation to the disclosure of personal information (the relevant personal information) about an individual by an APP entity to an overseas recipient if:
 (a) the recipient of the relevant personal information is:
 (i) subject to the laws of a country that is prescribed by the regulations; or
 (ii) a participant in a binding scheme that is prescribed by the regulations; and
 (b) if the country or binding scheme is prescribed subject to conditions—those conditions are satisfied.
Note: There are prerequisites that must be satisfied before the matters mentioned in this subclause are prescribed: see subsection 100(1A).

9.title: adoption, use or disclosure of government related identifiers
9.text:
9  Australian Privacy Principle 9—adoption, use or disclosure of government related identifiers
Adoption of government related identifiers
 9.1 An organisation must not adopt a government related identifier of an individual as its own identifier of the individual unless:
 (a) the adoption of the government related identifier is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order; or
 (b) subclause 9.3 applies in relation to the adoption.
Note: An act or practice of an agency may be treated as an act or practice of an organisation, see section 7A.
Use or disclosure of government related identifiers
 9.2 An organisation must not use or disclose a government related identifier of an individual unless:
 (a) the use or disclosure of the identifier is reasonably necessary for the organisation to verify the identity of the individual for the purposes of the organisation’s activities or functions; or
 (b) the use or disclosure of the identifier is reasonably necessary for the organisation to fulfil its obligations to an agency or a State or Territory authority; or
 (c) the use or disclosure of the identifier is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order; or
 (d) a permitted general situation (other than the situation referred to in item 4 or 5 of the table in subsection 16A(1)) exists in relation to the use or disclosure of the identifier; or
 (e) the organisation reasonably believes that the use or disclosure of the identifier is reasonably necessary for one or more enforcement related activities conducted by, or on behalf of, an enforcement body; or
 (f) subclause 9.3 applies in relation to the use or disclosure.
Note 1: An act or practice of an agency may be treated as an act or practice of an organisation, see section 7A.
Note 2: For permitted general situation, see section 16A.
Regulations about adoption, use or disclosure
 9.3 This subclause applies in relation to the adoption, use or disclosure by an organisation of a government related identifier of an individual if:
 (a) the identifier is prescribed by the regulations; and
 (b) the organisation is prescribed by the regulations, or is included in a class of organisations prescribed by the regulations; and
 (c) the adoption, use or disclosure occurs in the circumstances prescribed by the regulations.
Note: There are prerequisites that must be satisfied before the matters mentioned in this subclause are prescribed, see subsections 100(2) and (3).
Part 4—Integrity of personal information

10.title: quality of personal information
10.text:
10  Australian Privacy Principle 10—quality of personal information
 10.1 An APP entity must take such steps (if any) as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure that the personal information that the entity collects is accurate, up‑to‑date and complete.
 10.2 An APP entity must take such steps (if any) as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure that the personal information that the entity uses or discloses is, having regard to the purpose of the use or disclosure, accurate, up‑to‑date, complete and relevant.

11.title: security of personal information
11.text:
11  Australian Privacy Principle 11—security of personal information
 11.1 If an APP entity holds personal information, the entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to protect the information:
 (a) from misuse, interference and loss; and
 (b) from unauthorised access, modification or disclosure.
 11.2 If:
 (a) an APP entity holds personal information about an individual; and
 (b) the entity no longer needs the information for any purpose for which the information may be used or disclosed by the entity under this Schedule; and
 (c) the information is not contained in a Commonwealth record; and
 (d) the entity is not required by or under an Australian law, or a court/tribunal order, to retain the information;
the entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to destroy the information or to ensure that the information is de‑identified.
 11.3 For the purposes of subclauses 11.1 and 11.2, without limiting those subclauses or any other provision of this Act, such steps include technical and organisational measures.
Part 5—Access to, and correction of, personal information

12.title: access to personal information
12.text:
12  Australian Privacy Principle 12—access to personal information
Access
 12.1 If an APP entity holds personal information about an individual, the entity must, on request by the individual, give the individual access to the information.
Exception to access—agency
 12.2 If:
 (a) the APP entity is an agency; and
 (b) the entity is required or authorised to refuse to give the individual access to the personal information by or under:
 (i) the Freedom of Information Act; or
 (ii) any other Act of the Commonwealth, or a law in force in an external Territory, that provides for access by persons to documents;
then, despite subclause 12.1, the entity is not required to give access to the extent that the entity is required or authorised to refuse to give access.
Exception to access—organisation
 12.3 If the APP entity is an organisation then, despite subclause 12.1, the entity is not required to give the individual access to the personal information to the extent that:
 (a) the entity reasonably believes that giving access would pose a serious threat to the life, health or safety of any individual, or to public health or public safety; or
 (b) giving access would have an unreasonable impact on the privacy of other individuals; or
 (c) the request for access is frivolous or vexatious; or
 (d) the information relates to existing or anticipated legal proceedings between the entity and the individual, and would not be accessible by the process of discovery in those proceedings; or
 (e) giving access would reveal the intentions of the entity in relation to negotiations with the individual in such a way as to prejudice those negotiations; or
 (f) giving access would be unlawful; or
 (g) denying access is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order; or
 (h) both of the following apply:
 (i) the entity has reason to suspect that unlawful activity, or misconduct of a serious nature, that relates to the entity’s functions or activities has been, is being or may be engaged in;
 (ii) giving access would be likely to prejudice the taking of appropriate action in relation to the matter; or
 (i) giving access would be likely to prejudice one or more enforcement related activities conducted by, or on behalf of, an enforcement body; or
 (j) giving access would reveal evaluative information generated within the entity in connection with a commercially sensitive decision‑making process.
Dealing with requests for access
 12.4 The APP entity must:
 (a) respond to the request for access to the personal information:
 (i) if the entity is an agency—within 30 days after the request is made; or
 (ii) if the entity is an organisation—within a reasonable period after the request is made; and
 (b) give access to the information in the manner requested by the individual, if it is reasonable and practicable to do so.
Other means of access
 12.5 If the APP entity refuses:
 (a) to give access to the personal information because of subclause 12.2 or 12.3; or
 (b) to give access in the manner requested by the individual;
the entity must take such steps (if any) as are reasonable in the circumstances to give access in a way that meets the needs of the entity and the individual.
 12.6 Without limiting subclause 12.5, access may be given through the use of a mutually agreed intermediary.
Access charges
 12.7 If the APP entity is an agency, the entity must not charge the individual for the making of the request or for giving access to the personal information.
 12.8 If:
 (a) the APP entity is an organisation; and
 (b) the entity charges the individual for giving access to the personal information;
the charge must not be excessive and must not apply to the making of the request.
Refusal to give access
 12.9 If the APP entity refuses to give access to the personal information because of subclause 12.2 or 12.3, or to give access in the manner requested by the individual, the entity must give the individual a written notice that sets out:
 (a) the reasons for the refusal except to the extent that, having regard to the grounds for the refusal, it would be unreasonable to do so; and
 (b) the mechanisms available to complain about the refusal; and
 (c) any other matter prescribed by the regulations.
 12.10 If the APP entity refuses to give access to the personal information because of paragraph 12.3(j), the reasons for the refusal may include an explanation for the commercially sensitive decision.

13.title: correction of personal information
13.text:
13  Australian Privacy Principle 13—correction of personal information
Correction
 13.1 If:
 (a) an APP entity holds personal information about an individual; and
 (b) either:
 (i) the entity is satisfied that, having regard to a purpose for which the information is held, the information is inaccurate, out‑of‑date, incomplete, irrelevant or misleading; or
 (ii) the individual requests the entity to correct the information;
the entity must take such steps (if any) as are reasonable in the circumstances to correct that information to ensure that, having regard to the purpose for which it is held, the information is accurate, up‑to‑date, complete, relevant and not misleading.
Notification of correction to third parties
 13.2 If:
 (a) the APP entity corrects personal information about an individual that the entity previously disclosed to another APP entity; and
 (b) the individual requests the entity to notify the other APP entity of the correction;
the entity must take such steps (if any) as are reasonable in the circumstances to give that notification unless it is impracticable or unlawful to do so.
Refusal to correct information
 13.3 If the APP entity refuses to correct the personal information as requested by the individual, the entity must give the individual a written notice that sets out:
 (a) the reasons for the refusal except to the extent that it would be unreasonable to do so; and
 (b) the mechanisms available to complain about the refusal; and
 (c) any other matter prescribed by the regulations.
Request to associate a statement
 13.4 If:
 (a) the APP entity refuses to correct the personal information as requested by the individual; and
 (b) the individual requests the entity to associate with the information a statement that the information is inaccurate, out‑of‑date, incomplete, irrelevant or misleading;
the entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to associate the statement in such a way that will make the statement apparent to users of the information.
Dealing with requests
 13.5 If a request is made under subclause 13.1 or 13.4, the APP entity:
 (a) must respond to the request:
 (i) if the entity is an agency—within 30 days after the request is made; or
 (ii) if the entity is an organisation—within a reasonable period after the request is made; and
 (b) must not charge the individual for the making of the request, for correcting the personal information or for associating the statement with the personal information (as the case may be).
